headline: A judge halts the border wall at Big Bend. For now.
summary: Judge Kathleen Cardone blocked border wall work across the 500-mile Big Bend sector of Texas on Friday, national park included. An environmental group, a church's supporters and a river guide sued after the government waived the laws that protect the land. Bulldozers cleared ground in the park in August. The order holds until she rules.

cover_question.q: Can one judge really stop the wall?

cover_answer: Yes, until the trial. The bulldozers wait.
table_question: If a rule slows you down, is it ever OK to skip it?

5-7.chip: Bring it up if it fits the day
5-7.script: The government started building a tall steel fence through a park in Texas, next to a river with cliffs. Today a judge said stop, until a court decides whether the rules were followed. The fence would be as tall as five grown-ups standing on each other's shoulders. The park is still there, and the grown-ups have it.
5-7.why: A fence and a stop sign. Six-year-olds know what those do.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old reasons from what is in front of them, so the script gives them a fence and a stop sign. Five grown-ups on each other's shoulders is the anchor: a wall they can picture against a park they cannot. Nothing here is frightening, and the script keeps it that way. Expect "will they build it anyway?" Not until a court says so.

8-12.script: Building a wall through a national park means following laws that protect the land. The government waived them to go faster. A park group, a church's friends and a river guide sued, and on Friday a judge stopped the work until the case is decided. A whistle, not the final score.
8-12.why: Laws skipped, a suit, a whistle. Not the score.
8-12.why_long: This age is working out whether adults follow the rules they set, so the script hands them the chain: laws waived, a suit filed, a judge's whistle. The referee is the mechanism, and a whistle is a pause, not a verdict. Expect "so did the government cheat?" The other side will probably win a point, and that is enough to stop play.

13-17.script: Is "remote and rugged" a border defence? Big Bend has the fewest crossings of nine sectors, and the government skipped environmental laws there to build faster. A judge halted the work Friday. Second: the government's lawyers called no witnesses. Why?
13-17.why: The border is a real job; so were the skipped laws.
13-17.why_long: A teenager can hold two true things at once: the border is the government's to secure, and the laws it waived were there for a reason. The script asks whether a canyon can be a wall, then the empty witness chair: data on one side, silence on the other. Expect "so the judge is political?" A Bush appointee wrote the order. Temporary, too.

5-7.q: Why do they want a fence there?
5-7.a: To stop people crossing from Mexico. The judge said they can't build it until the court has looked at how they went about it.

8-12.q: Can one judge really stop the wall?
8-12.a: Yes, for now. Work stops across the sector until the case ends.

8-12.q: Why did the government skip the laws?
8-12.a: To go faster. Crossings there are the fewest of nine sectors.

13-17.q: Is this the end of the wall there?
13-17.a: No. A pause until the trial. The agency stands by its authority.

13-17.q: Does a wall even matter in Big Bend?
13-17.a: Opponents say the canyons do it. No park numbers were supplied.
